segments.say: Let's go back to something simpler than a face, and shorter than a sentence. One small word, spoken once, to someone you've never met.

Felix has just remembered another small thing. Three weeks ago, before he'd even started, he phoned the studio to confirm his start date. A man answered, and said, hello, studio, in a low, easy voice. That was Jonas. It was the first thing Felix ever heard from the place. And he remembers, now, that he'd felt, immediately, a small, relaxed warmth.

Think how little that was. Two words, and one of them hardly counts, because it was only the name of the place. And yet something in Felix had made a quiet judgment about the man behind them. He sounded friendly. He sounded like someone you could ask a silly question. And all of it came from the sound of a single, ordinary hello.

It's the sort of thing that psychologists ask. How much does a voice tell us, if all we've heard is one word? Not a speech, and not a conversation. Just hello, the most common word in the world, and the one that most of us say before anything else.

In 2014, three researchers, McAleer, Todorov and Belin, published a study in the journal PLoS ONE with a title that made it very clear. How do you say hello? They recorded sixty-four young people from Scotland, thirty-two men and thirty-two women, each saying the word hello, and cut out that single word. It lasted about four tenths of a second.

show.what: Three hundred and twenty listeners rated recordings of the word hello, about 0.4 seconds long, spoken by 64 Scottish students, 32 men and 32 women, on personality traits such as trustworthiness and dominance.

segments.say: Then three hundred and twenty people, listening online, heard those short clips and rated each voice, on personality traits such as how trustworthy it sounded, how dominant, and how attractive. It was a very short thing to rate. Four tenths of a second is about as long as it takes to say the word aloud.

Here's the number that matters. Four tenths of a second. And the finding was that the listeners' ratings agreed with one another. People didn't give random scores. They tended to hear the same things in the same voices, even in a word that short, which is part of what makes a first impression feel so shared and so obvious.

show.title: McAleer et al., 2014
show.label: the length of the single word hello that listeners rated on personality

segments.say: When the team looked at how the ratings fitted together, a tidy pattern appeared. The traits clustered into two big dimensions. The first was about whether a voice seemed friendly and trustworthy, which the researchers call valence. The second was about whether it seemed strong and in charge, which they call dominance. A whole space of impressions, in just two directions.

They also looked at attractiveness. For male voices, sounding more attractive went with both valence and dominance, and dominance counted for more. For female voices, attractiveness was driven mainly by valence, the friendly, trustworthy side. In other words, the two dimensions didn't mean quite the same thing in the two sets of voices.

show.title: The social voice space
items: Men's voices seemed more attractive with both, and dominance counted more
Women's voices seemed more attractive mainly with valence

segments.say: The team also measured the sounds themselves. Things like the pitch of the voice, how clear and smooth it was compared with how breathy or rough, and how its resonances were spread. Some of these measurements predicted some of the ratings. So the impressions weren't simply made up from nothing. They were connected, in part, to real, measurable features of the voice.

But the note of care applies here too. The study shows that listeners agree in their impressions of a very short voice clip. It doesn't show that a voice with a particular pitch belongs to a trustworthy person. The raters were making impressions, and the researchers were measuring how those impressions were organised. Whether the impressions were true was a different question.

Here's a quiet, old-fashioned picture. A telephone on a small wooden table, in a hallway, with a lamp beside it. Before it rings, it's only an object. After one word comes down the line, it's the beginning of an impression. A whole person is imagined from a fraction of a second of sound.

Felix thinks about Jonas's hello. And he realises that his warmth toward Jonas started three weeks earlier than he'd thought. It began with a voice, on a phone, in a four-tenths-of-a-second word. By the time he walked in and saw the grin, the mug and the stack of plants, he'd already half decided. The face, the grin and the mug simply agreed with a voice.

That's a pattern worth noticing. Impressions from different channels tend to agree with one another, and agreement feels like confirmation. A friendly voice, then a friendly face, then a friendly mug. Three sources, and they all say the same thing. But they weren't three independent witnesses. They were three slices of the same impression, each leaning on the one before.

It's a useful distinction. When a verdict arrives from several directions, it feels very solid. But if the first impression coloured the later ones, then the agreement is partly an echo. The mind rarely checks for that. It simply registers that everything fits, and feels reassured.

show.text: Three slices that agree are not three independent proofs.

segments.say: Felix wonders what Mara's voice might have said, if he'd heard it first, on a phone, before the word cold was in his head. He doesn't know. It's impossible to rewind. But he's starting to suspect that the brisk tone he'd taken as a sign of coldness might have sounded, on another day, like someone who is efficient, and perhaps a little nervous about being kind.

It's a charitable thought, and he's not sure he believes it yet. But it's a possible one. Plenty of people who sound brisk are nervous, or busy, or shy, or simply hungry. A voice is a lovely clue, and a poor biography. It tells you something about a moment, and leaves the rest to be found out.

Of course Mara has been doing the same thing to him. His voice, on the phone, three weeks ago. His handshake, his bag, his I'm so happy to be here. She has made her own quick sketch, and she's carrying it around too, probably with about as much evidence. It's a small, steadying thought. Everyone in that building has been forming impressions all day, and none of us knows how well.

There's something rather companionable in that. Two people, on either side of a glass door, each forming a hasty picture of the other, each partly wrong. It's not a problem to be solved tonight. It's just a very human arrangement, and it's far less lonely than it seemed an hour ago.
So we've seen how fast they form, and how widely they spread. Now the big question. When we form a quick impression, how often is it correct?

Take a slow breath in, and let it out gently. Felix lets his eyes close, and imagines the sound of a telephone ringing, far away, in a quiet hallway. He doesn't answer it. He just listens, and lets the ringing fade, and the silence afterwards feels full and warm.
